summary: For ages 9–11: learners build an understanding of the cryosphere as all of Earth's frozen water (ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, snow cover), grasp that most of Earth's fresh water is frozen (polar ice sheets hold roughly 68–69% per cited sources), and learn that the cryosphere is a live store connected to oceans and atmosphere through the water cycle. A central discriminating idea: melting land-based ice is what raises sea level noticeably, because floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water (in the real salty ocean, melting sea ice adds only a very tiny rise). Activities range from a manipulable store-and-flow model and a labelled component map to a hands-on displacement demonstration and a companion recognition/estimate check.
misconceptions: Most of Earth's fresh water is in rivers and lakes — the great majority is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers
The cryosphere is just 'ice at the poles' — it also includes glaciers, permafrost, snow cover and sea ice worldwide
Frozen water is separate from the water cycle — it is a major store connected by evaporation, snowfall and meltwater
Melting any ice raises sea level equally — only land ice adds water; floating sea ice does not raise it
The ice is a permanent, unchanging block — it constantly exchanges water with oceans and atmosphere

activities.title: Frozen Earth console: melt it and watch the system respond
steps: Study a display of the planet's water as two proportion bars — a large salty-sea bar and, within the small fresh-water sliver, a bar showing that most fresh water is frozen.
Explore a map of cryosphere components: ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost, and snow cover.

Melt components one at a time and observe a sea-level gauge: melting floating Arctic sea ice leaves the gauge still; melting the Greenland and Antarctic ice SHEETS makes it climb toward a marked ~65 m level (per cited sources: Greenland ~7.4 m + Antarctica ~58 m).
Watch water-cycle arrows respond as you act — evaporation, snowfall rebuilding glaciers, and meltwater rivers flowing to the sea — showing ice as a live store, not a static block.
State in your own words why the frozen sliver matters and why only land ice lifts the sea.
activities.insight: The cryosphere is a giant connected reservoir holding most of Earth's fresh water; it exchanges water with oceans and atmosphere through the water cycle, and only land-based ice raises sea level when it melts.

activities.title: Cryosphere map and water-store proportion bars
steps: Label a component map identifying ice sheets, glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover.
Examine proportion bars for salt vs fresh water, and frozen vs liquid fresh water; optionally tap-to-reveal the key figures.
State which store holds most of Earth's fresh water and name three parts of the cryosphere.
activities.insight: The cryosphere is a named umbrella term with distinct components worldwide, and most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in the ice sheets and glaciers.

activities.title: Displacement demo: floating ice vs land ice
steps: Fill a glass to the brim with water and float an ice cube in it.

Predict, WITH A REASON, whether the glass will overflow as the floating cube melts, then let it melt and observe whether the level changes (it should stay at about the same level; wipe the outside of the glass so condensation is not mistaken for overflow).
Let meltwater from a cube resting on a spoon or saucer lip (standing for land ice) run into the glass, and observe that this overflows.
Compare the two cases and explain why floating ice behaves differently from land ice.
Transfer to a new case: decide whether Greenland's land ice or floating Arctic sea ice matters more for rising seas, and say why.
activities.insight: Floating ice already displaces its own weight of water, so in this fresh-water demo melting it keeps the level about the same (in the salty ocean, melting sea ice adds only a very tiny rise); land-based ice adds new water to the sea. Mass is conserved — melting changes state and location, not the amount of water.

activities.title: Companion check: name, estimate, and distinguish
steps: Name three parts of the cryosphere.
Use a proportion estimate (e.g. a slider) to indicate how much of Earth's fresh water is frozen.
Answer land-vs-sea-ice questions about which melting ice raises sea level and why.
activities.insight: Consolidates the vocabulary, the proportion figure, and the land-vs-sea-ice distinction.

activities.title: Glaciologist's account of the cryosphere (optional discussion)
steps: Listen to or read a short account of the cryosphere's components and its role connecting ice to oceans and atmosphere.
Ask questions and respond: where is most frozen water, and why does only land ice raise the sea?
activities.insight: The cryosphere is a connected store at the heart of the water cycle; changes there ripple globally to sea level, currents and water supply.

checkQuestion: Two big ice cubes are melting. One is floating in a glass of water filled right to the brim. The other is sitting on a saucer next to the glass. When both have melted, which one — if either — makes water spill over the edge of the glass? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: The floating ice cube will NOT make the glass overflow — floating ice already pushes aside (displaces) exactly its own weight of water, so when it melts it just fills the space it was displacing and the level stays the same. The ice on the saucer stands for land ice (glaciers and ice sheets on land): if its meltwater ran into the glass it WOULD raise the level. So only melting LAND ice raises sea level; melting floating sea ice does not.
